title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E420 is Euler's 1771/72 reworking of the calculus of variations in his 'variation' (δ) formalism. He classifies integrands Z(x,y,p,q), with p=y' and q=y'', according to the order of the resulting curve equation. Writing dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq, he treats the third class on this page.

(§52) The third class is the case where Q itself contains q, so Z depends genuinely and nonlinearly on y''. The curve equation is 0 = N − d/dx P + d²/dx² Q. In modern terms this is the Euler–Poisson equation ∂Z/∂y − (∂Z/∂y')' + (∂Z/∂y'')'' = 0. Here d²Q/dx² contains fourth derivatives of y, so the solution has four arbitrary constants. These let one prescribe both endpoints and the tangent directions at both endpoints, i.e. clamped boundary data y(a), y'(a), y(b), y'(b). This is contrasted with §51 on the previous page, where Z is linear in q (Z = Z₀ + Ƶ q). There the q-term is a null-Lagrangian-type contribution and the equation collapses to second order.

(§53) Illustration: the elastic curve. With ρ the radius of curvature at M, Euler states that elastic curves make ∫ ds/ρ² = ∫ dx √(1+p²)/ρ² a minimum. Using ρ = (1+p²)^{3/2}/q he gets Z = q²/(1+p²)^{5/2}. Hence:
- M = 0 and N = 0;
- P = ∂Z/∂p = −5pq²/(1+p²)^{7/2};
- Q = ∂Z/∂q = 2q/(1+p²)^{5/2}.
Since N = 0, the equation is 0 = −dP/dx + d²Q/dx².

Continuation on the next page:
- A first integral is P − dQ/dx = A (momentum conservation, since y is cyclic).
- Multiplying by dp = q dx and using dZ = P dp + Q dq gives the second first integral Z − qQ = Ap + B. This is the Hamiltonian/energy integral from x-independence, mixed with the first integral.
- This yields q² = (Ap+B)(1+p²)^{5/2}, then dx = dp/((1+p²)^{5/4}√(Ap+B)) and dy = p dp/(same).

In tangent-angle form (p = tanθ) the curvature is κ = q/(1+p²)^{3/2}, which gives κ² = A sinθ + B cosθ. This is the pendulum-type elastica equation from Euler's 1744 Additamentum I.
errors: The computations of Z, P and Q on this page are correct: 1/ρ² = q²/(1+p²)³, so Z = q²/(1+p²)^{5/2}; P = −5pq²(1+p²)^{−7/2}; Q = 2q(1+p²)^{−5/2}.

Conceptual gap: Euler says that all elastic curves ('omnes hae curvae') minimize ∫ds/ρ² outright. In the 1744 Methodus inveniendi (Additamentum I, following Daniel Bernoulli) this holds only under the isoperimetric constraint of fixed arc length. Without the multiplier term λ√(1+p²), the integration on the next page gives κ² = A sinθ + B cosθ, with no additive constant. That is only the 'rectangular' elastica, the λ=0 free elastica. The general family κ² = A sinθ + B cosθ + C needs the length constraint. So the example, as posed here, does not yield 'all' elastic curves. Euler does not remark on this.
Minor: the sign change of constants ('mutatis signis') is legitimate. Requiring Ap+B ≥ 0 is implicit.

ideas.what: Euler–Poisson equation for integrands depending on y''; fourth order with four constants fixing endpoints and end tangents
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Poisson equation; clamped boundary conditions for higher-order variational problems
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi 1744), Poisson's name attached later
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (E65, 1744), ch. II–III; also Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385)

ideas.what: Order classification by whether Q = ∂Z/∂q depends on q (contrast with linear-in-q case of §51)
ideas.modern_name: degenerate (affine in highest derivative) Lagrangians / null Lagrangian reduction

ideas.what: Elastica as minimizer of ∫ds/ρ² (bending energy), integrand q²/(1+p²)^{5/2}
ideas.modern_name: Euler elastica / Bernoulli bending energy (Willmore-type curve energy)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli (suggestion, 1742) and Euler (1744 Additamentum I)

ideas.what: Two first integrals: P − Q' = A (y cyclic) and Z − qQ = Ap + B (x absent), reducing to quadrature
ideas.modern_name: Noether-type conserved quantities (translation invariance), Hamiltonian of second-order Lagrangian

deep.surprise_reason: This is a textbook re-derivation of the Euler–Poisson equation and the elastica, both well documented since 1744. The only notable point is that the length constraint is omitted, which silently restricts the result to the rectangular elastica. That is an oversight, not a new result, and the free-elastica fact is well known in modern literature (e.g. Langer–Singer).
